edition: Issue #006 — Letterboxd courts the big-money suitors, Margot Robbie trades her surname, and the humble tarakihi becomes the nation's most argued-about fish
tagline: Your 3-minute break. Zero fluff, maximum banter.

stories.headline: Letterboxd eyes the big money: the New York Times is one of three suitors
stories.summary: Auckland-founded film-social app Letterboxd is reportedly in play, with the New York Times among three suitors and a valuation of more than US$300m that could hand its Kiwi founders a reported $206m payday.

body.text: The Auckland-founded film-tracking app Letterboxd, where millions of us log every movie we've ever sighed through, is reportedly in takeover talks. The New York Times is one of three suitors circling, with the company said to be valued at more than US$300 million. The Herald reports a deal could deliver the Kiwi founders a payday of around $206 million — a lot of money for an app whose core business model is letting people write slightly-too-long reviews nobody asked for.

The New York Times, keeper of the crossword and the 52-point Times New Roman front page, gearing up to own your Letterboxd diary is like your local library buying the fish-and-chip shop down the road. And for the founders — two blokes who turned a hobby for rating films into a nine-figure cheque — the big lesson is that the one app you're scared to admit you spend your Sunday morning on is apparently worth more than some actual whole countries. Wake up and smell the arbitrarily-expensive snack: somebody's about to pay you to never have to think about a paddock again.

NZ Herald (25 Sep 2026), citing the paper's reporting: Letterboxd, the film-logging social platform founded in Auckland, is reported to have interest from three suitors including The New York Times, with the company valued at more than US$300 million. The Herald reported the deal could deliver the Auckland founders a payout of approximately $206 million (NZD). Independent tech coverage described the field as A24, Sony, or The New York Times closing in on Letterboxd. Figures are as reported by NZ Herald and not yet confirmed as final sale terms.

stories.headline: Margot Robbie is now Margot Ackerley — and the internet has strong feelings
stories.summary: Ten years after marrying producer Tom Ackerley, the Barbie star has formally changed her name to Margot Ackerley on the couple's LuckyChap Entertainment company documents, triggering a flood of hot takes online.

body.text: Australian actress Margot Robbie has changed her name to Margot Ackerley — a decade after marrying her husband, British producer Tom Ackerley. UK Companies House documents show the Barbie star has switched from her maiden name Robbie to her married name, and the couple's production company LuckyChap Entertainment now lists the co-founder as Margot Ackerley. It's not yet clear whether she'll keep going by Robbie in her career, but the paperwork change could signal a shift. Online, the reaction has been loud.

The discourse committee has spoken and the verdict is in: a woman who has been legally free to file this form for ten years has finally filed it, and the internet has somehow turned it into a referendum on feminism, branding, and the exact emotional weight of a hyphen. Somewhere out there a man with the letter-to-the-editor energy of a rotary phone is explaining that changing your name is basically a bad business decision, as though Margot Robbie's chattel value weren't now literally stamped on a company registry in a way he can check. The real story is the guy who said the quiet part loud: her mama named her Margot Robbie, and he's calling her Margot Robbie whether Companies House likes it or not.

NZ Herald (25 Sep 2026): UK Companies House records show Margot Robbie has formally changed her name to Margot Ackerley, 10 years after marrying Tom Ackerley (married since 2016); LuckyChap Entertainment, the couple's production company, now lists the co-founder as Margot Ackerley. The couple welcomed a baby boy in October 2024. The Herald reported fan reaction online, including social posts calling the change a bad business decision and Barbie would never take a man's surname. It noted it is unclear whether the actress will continue using her maiden name professionally.

stories.headline: Ten tarakihi per person: the great Kiwi fish limit battle drags on
stories.summary: Fisheries Minister Shane Jones has slashed tarakihi catch limits — 10 per person nationwide for recreational fishers, with commercial catches cut 20% on the east and 55% on the west — but campaigners say it's not enough and are threatening legal action.

body.text: Fisheries Minister Shane Jones has cut tarakihi catch limits: recreational fishers are now limited to 10 per person nationwide, while commercial limits drop 20 percent in the eastern fishery and a hefty 55 percent in the west. The minister says the moves are based on the latest science and will reduce pressure on depleted stocks. But environmental groups are unimpressed — the Environmental Defence Society says the eastern tarakihi stock sits at just 7.7 percent of its estimated original biomass, well below the 10 percent threshold where closure should be on the table, and it is exploring legal action. LegaSea says the cuts don't go far enough.

Finally, a use for the maths we all abandoned in year nine: you are now legally permitted to catch exactly ten tarakihi and not one more, because a panel of blokes in Wellington offices and a lot of very opinionated fish scientists have decided that's the precise number the sea can spare this year. It's peak Kiwi that one of our most fought-over national resources is a fish you have to actively go out and wrestle off a line to even complain about — and that the fight to save it has turned into two sides both waving clipboards of evidence at each other like it's a rugby scrum. If the fish could vote, they'd presumably join the side shouting leave me alone, actually. Meanwhile everyone's favourite fisheries scientist, the bloke who'll correct you in the queue at the fish counter, is having the week of his life.

RNZ (22 Sep 2026): Fisheries Minister Shane Jones announced tarakihi catch limits would be cut, including a nationwide recreational limit of 10 per person; commercial limits are reduced by 20 percent in the eastern fishery and 55 percent in the western fishery. Butterfish were cut to a 5-per-person recreational limit. The Environmental Defence Society (EDS) said eastern tarakihi is at 7.7% of its estimated original biomass — below the 10 hard limit where closure is an option — and that western tarakihi is at approximately 29% of unfished biomass yet in rapid decline; EDS sought a total fishery closure and said it is investigating legal options to challenge the decision. LegaSea's Benn Winlove said the 20% east-coast cut does not cut it and further court cases should be expected (Forest and Bird and the Environmental Law Initiative have previously taken court action). Limits were increased for snapper and trevally on the North Island's east coast and other stocks.
